title: SIM-CaliRam: A workflow combining simulation-informed references and biomass-augmented features for in-line Raman calibration of Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
abstract: Raman spectroscopy is a promising in-situ Process Analytical Technology for upstream bioprocesses, but transferring trained calibration models to new, independent fermentation runs without re-calibration remains a challenge due to sparse sample references (SaR) and prediction drift caused by biomass-induced fluorescence and turbidity effects. We present SIM-CaliRam, a calibration workflow combining two physically motivated interventions.

title: Engineering Synergistic Sites in a Cerium-Based Metal–Organic Framework for Photocatalytic CO2 Reduction
abstract: Photoreduction of CO2 to produce solar fuels is an important target. Redox-active Ce-based metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) are promising catalysts. Herein, we have synthesized an amino-functionalized Ce-based MOF, PKU-167 (PKU = Peking University). Upon introduction of Co(bpy)2Cl2 (bpy = 2,2′-bipyridine) to the skeleton of PKU-167, PKU-167-0.9Co achieved a high CO production rate of 18.4 mmol g–1 h–1 with a selectivity of 91.8% under visible-light irradiation and an apparent quantum yield of 1.97% at 425 nm.

title: Bee nest linings could inspire plastics that break down in soil
abstract: Hundreds of millions of metric tons of plastics are produced every year, and most of them end up sitting in landfills or polluting natural environments after use. These plastics endure for dozens to hundreds of years. But some scientists are on the lookout for solutions to this problem. And now, one team of researchers might have found a potential solution in bee nests. Their study, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, shows that a natural plastic made by bees may offer design lessons for plastics that degrade naturally in far less time.

title: Predictive nanotoxicology of graphene-family nanomaterials: Standardised descriptors, explainable machine learning and safe-by-design
abstract: Graphene-family nanomaterials (GFNs) comprise structurally and chemically diverse two-dimensional materials with broad applications in biomedicine, environmental technologies, energy, sensing, and advanced materials. Their expanding use has increased the need for reliable approaches to characterize and predict potential biological and environmental hazards. However, meaningful comparison of GFN toxicity data remains difficult because biological responses depend on interacting material characteristics, including lateral dimensions, layer number, defects, oxidation, surface functionalization, charge, morphology, aggregation, and dispersion state, together with exposure conditions, dosimetry, biological models, and endpoint definitions. This review examines how standardized descriptors can provide a quantitative basis for connecting GFN characteristics with toxicological responses and constructing reproducible predictive datasets. Structural, chemical, surface, colloidal, electronic, computational, exposure and biological descriptors are considered within an integrated framework that distinguishes intrinsic material properties from exposure-state characteristics. Particular emphasis is placed on descriptor harmonization, dataset curation, data provenance, and consistent reporting of measurement and dose information. The review also discusses machine-learning approaches for modelling nonlinear and multidimensional relationships between GFN descriptors and toxicity, emphasising the significance of proper feature selection, validation, applicability-domain assessment and uncertainty quantification. Because GFN datasets may contain limited numbers of independently characterized materials and substantial variation in experimental protocols, predictive performance should be interpreted in the context of data quality, validation design, and applicability-domain limitations. Explainable machine learning is considered as a means of identifying influential descriptors and generating mechanistically testable hypotheses rather than causal conclusions. Building on these principles, a standardized predictive framework is proposed that links characterization, descriptor harmonization, toxicity datasets, validated and explainable machine learning, experimental confirmation, and iterative model refinement. The framework provides a foundation for using predictive insights to guide material modification and support Safe-by-Design and Safe-and-Sustainable-by-Design strategies. Overall, standardized descriptors and traceable data practices can help advance GFN nanotoxicology from heterogeneous retrospective comparisons toward reproducible, interpretable, and experimentally testable prediction.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Prediction and Optimization of Methylene Blue Adsorption onto Albizia lebbeck Bio-adsorbent Using Ensemble Machine Learning
abstract: This study investigates the adsorption of methylene blue (MB)from aqueous solution using a bio-adsorbent prepared from Albizialebbeck pods and evaluates the predictive performance of ensemble machine learning models for modeling the adsorption process. The bio-adsorbent was characterized using pH PZC , Fourier Transform Infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), X-ray Diffraction (XRD),and Scanning Electron Microscopy with Energy Dispersive Spectroscopy (SEM–EDS).

title: Oil-producing yeast reveals two stages of fat accumulation under nitrogen limitation
abstract: A research team led by professors Xu Guowang and Liu Xinyu from the Dalian Institute of Chemical Physics (DICP) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS), in collaboration with researchers from Dalian University of Technology, has developed a high-coverage lipidomics workflow and integrated it with transcriptomics to investigate lipid accumulation and compositional changes in Rhodosporidium toruloides under nitrogen limitation. The study was recently published in Food Chemistry.

title: The Stress Localization Function─A Stress-Derived Real-Space Descriptor for Chemical Bonding Analysis
abstract: Existing quantum-chemical topology descriptors, including the Laplacian of the electron density, the Electron Localization Function (ELF), and the Localized Orbital Locator (LOL), characterize bonding through the density and its low-order derivatives, but they trace the localization of electrons rather than the local balance between the kinetic and potential energy densities and sometimes fail in cases such as heavy atoms, hypervalent centers, and bonds of intermediate character. To address these deficiencies, we introduce the Stress Localization Function (SLF), a real-space bonding descriptor constructed from the quantum-mechanical stress tensor. The trace of the stress tensor is the local virial field, which connects the kinetic and potential energy at each point in space. The SLF is obtained by taking its magnitude, comparing it to the value for a uniform electron gas of the same local density, and mapping the result onto a bounded scale, in analogy to the ELF or LOL. Applied to atoms across the periodic table, the SLF resolves the complete electronic shell structure, including the outermost shells of heavy atoms that the Laplacian fails to recover and that stress-based indicators have not resolved with any single choice of parameter. For the 4d elements, the SLF recovers the full complement of shells with no adjustable parameter. It registers the number of occupied shells rather than the nominal period, as shown by palladium’s anomalous 4d105s0 configuration. The core value is essentially universal (≈0.578), transferable from free atoms to bonded environments. Across a benchmark set of single, double, and triple bonds, the SLF decreases monotonically with bond order while simultaneously tracking bond polarity through the electronegativity of the bonding partner, separating two distinct chemical effects within a single scalar field. The descriptor further characterizes nonprototypical bonding, including three-center bonds, as in the textbook example of H3+ and boranes, the hypervalent center in BrF3, and the σ-donation and π-back-donation of metal carbonyls. The SLF thus provides a stress-derived, energetic view of electron organization that complements existing density-based descriptors.

title: Capturing Transient Polaron Formation Dynamics: A Time-Dependent Polaron Transformation Approach
abstract: Static polaron transformations impose an equilibrium environmental displacement at the initial time and can therefore misrepresent transient polaron formation. We introduce a time-dependent (TD) polaron transformation that describes the dynamical formation of polarons. We first present the TD polaron transformation for the spin–boson model via an infinite sequence of interaction-picture transformations.

title: Facile Maleimide-Hydrazine Reaction to Form Stable Bonds in Dynamic Hydrazone-Cross-Linked Hydrogels

title: Solid-Phase Capture of Phage for Combinatorial Chemical Diversification of Peptide Libraries
abstract: The chemical and structural diversity of peptide phage or mRNA-display libraries can be expanded by chemical modification, such as with cyclization reagents or by incorporation of unnatural amino acids, but the number of different non-natural building blocks introduced has been modest so far. To expand the chemical diversity in peptide display libraries, we developed a strategy for efficient parallel chemical diversification of phage display libraries based on capturing phage on a solid support via a polyhistidine tag and chemical modification. We applied chemically diverse building blocks in a 96-well format that allowed high-throughput experimentation, including parallel phage panning. Selections against the oncology target MCL-1 identified binders containing unnatural building blocks that were important for binding, such as thienylpyridine. This demonstrated the effectiveness of the approach and emphasized the advantages of an increased chemical diversity. This strategy may be particularly attractive for generating short peptide-based ligands, where the number of combinations based on proteinaceous amino acids is limited, for generating membrane-permeable peptides required for oral application or intracellular targeting.
